skill.name: Order the sentences into a paragraph
skill.why: Sentences in the wrong order confuse readers, even when every sentence is fine.
skill.how: Find the sentence that needs nothing before it. Then follow the clues: it, then, but.

beats.say: Every sentence leaves clues about what came before it.
Words like he, it and they point back.
Words like then and but link to the sentence before.
beats.show: Gus fixed it. **Then** it exploded again.

beats.say: So start with the sentence that needs nothing before it.
beats.show: **A girl called Nell** found a key.

beats.say: Then follow the clues, one link at a time.

Inside the jar was a lump of green slime.
The slime smelled exactly like Mo's footy socks.
Gus hid the jar inside one of those socks.
body.reason: Start with the sentence that needs nothing before it. Then follow the clues: the jar, the slime, those socks.

weDo.frame: Tully is sorting sentences for a story about the storm.
weDo.prompt: Could each sentence start a paragraph? Match each one.
weDo.hint: Look at the first word. Does it point back to something?
weDo.success: 'It', 'Then' and 'However' point back, so those sentences need one before them.

items.text: However, nobody was hurt.
items.reason: 'However' links to something before. Nobody was hurt in what?

creature.name: Queuepillar
creature.blurb: Bag-shelter moth caterpillars from the snow gums that march nose to tail in one long line. Each one follows the clue left by the one in front.

encounters.frame: Wren is reading the Queuepillars a bedtime story. The pages got muddled.
encounters.prompt: Put Wren's sentences in order.
encounters.success: Each sentence picks up something from the one before: the wombat, the scarf, the smell, then awake.

items: Wren found a baby wombat in the snow.
She wrapped the wombat in her red scarf.
The scarf smelled of Mo's burnt pancakes.
That smell woke the wombat right up.
Wide awake now, it licked Wren's nose.
body.reason: Start with the sentence that needs nothing before it. Then follow the clues: the wombat, the scarf, that smell.

encounters.frame: The Queuepillars marched over Gus's robot story and mixed it up.
encounters.prompt: Put the story about Gus's robot in order.
encounters.success: Every sentence links back to the one before: he, Clank, the toast, then the burnt toast.

items: Gus built a robot out of old tins.
He called the robot Clank.
Clank's first job was to make toast.
But the toast came out black and smoking.
Clank ate the burnt toast himself and burped smoke.
body.reason: 'He' needs Gus first. 'Clank' needs the naming. 'The toast' needs the job. 'Burnt' needs the smoke.

encounters.frame: A space comic blew into the Queuepillars' snow gum. Its sentences are muddled.
encounters.prompt: Put the space story in order.
encounters.success: Each sentence picks up the last one's new idea: the dust, then the floating dust, then the glint.

items: Captain Rosa Lim was the first person ever to land on the moon Pellucia.
As soon as she stepped out, her boots sank into soft blue dust.
The dust was so light that it floated up around her like smoke.
Through that floating dust, she spotted something glinting near a crater.
It was a gold sticker that said MAXX WAS HERE.
body.reason: Start with the captain. Then follow the clues: she, the dust, that floating dust, something glinting.

encounters.frame: Gus's slime recipe got shuffled. The Queuepillars are not touching it.
encounters.prompt: Put Gus's slime recipe in order.
encounters.success: Each step picks up the last one: the glue, the pea soup, the drops. 'Finally' comes last.

items: To make Gus's Famous Snot Slime, start by pouring a cup of glue into a bowl.
Stir a spoonful of green paint into the glue until it looks like pea soup.
Once the mixture looks like pea soup, add the activator one drop at a time.
When the drops have turned it thick and stringy, knead it with your hands.
Finally, leave your slime in the fridge overnight so it gets extra gloopy.
body.reason: 'Start by' begins the recipe. Then follow the clues: the glue, pea soup, the drops, and 'Finally'.

encounters.frame: Mo is singing at the Snow Festival. The Queuepillars are in the front row.
encounters.text: The Peaks Snow Festival had a stage made of ice, a choir of forty kids and a brass band that never stopped. Every year, someone was chosen to sing the festival song to open the show. This year, it was Mo's turn. He was so excited that he forgot to eat breakfast, which had never happened before. He wore his best beanie and a bow tie made of tinsel. When the band started, Mo stepped up to the microphone and took a huge breath. He had practised every night for three weeks, in the shower, on the ladders and once in his sleep.
encounters.prompt: Which sentence should come next?
encounters.success: 'However' sets up a surprise after all that practice. It links straight back to the sentence before.

options.text: She clapped so hard that both of her mittens flew off.
options.reason: 'She' has to point back to someone, but no girl or woman has been named yet.

options.text: However, he had practised the wrong song the whole time.
The second verse was even worse than the first.
options.reason: 'Even worse' means the first verse went badly. Mo hasn't sung a note yet.

encounters.success: Each sentence grabs something new from the one before: the frozen ball, the umpire, his whistle.

items: Last Saturday, the Peaks Under-12s played their first ever game of snow footy.
Nobody had warned them that the ball would freeze solid by half-time.
That frozen ball bounced off Tully's boot like a rock and hit the umpire.
The umpire, who was wearing three beanies, didn't feel a thing.
However, he was so cross that he blew the whistle for the end of the game.
That final whistle sent both teams inside for hot chips, still arguing about the score.
body.reason: Follow the chain: the team, that frozen ball, the umpire, 'However', then that final whistle.

encounters.frame: Gus wrote an explanation of his new robot. The Queuepillars knocked it over.
encounters.prompt: Put Gus's explanation in order.
encounters.success: Each sentence uses something from the one before: the Shovelator, the brushes, the bag, the creek.

items: Gus has invented a robot that clears snow from the ladders of Scaffold Peaks.
He calls it the Shovelator, and it is about the size of a wheelie bin.
On its front, the Shovelator has two spinning brushes made from old toothbrushes.
These brushes flick the snow off each rung and into a bag on the robot's back.
When the bag is full, the robot climbs down and empties it into the creek.
Once, it emptied the whole bag on the Architect instead of into the creek.
body.reason: 'He calls it' needs the robot. Then follow the clues: the Shovelator, these brushes, the bag, the creek.

encounters.frame: Indi's paragraph about her tower mural got jumbled. The Queuepillars want to know where to start.
encounters.text: Indi wrote a paragraph about the biggest painting she has ever done, but she dropped the cards on the way to the printer. Now the sentences are jumbled, and only one of them can come first. Indi wants the paragraph to make sense to someone who has never heard of the mural, so the first sentence has to set everything up. Here are the cards, in the order they landed on the floor. It took her eleven days, four ladders and nineteen tins of paint. On the twelfth day, she finally climbed down and saw the whole thing for the first time. Indi had been asked to paint a mural on the side of the Architect's tallest tower. The Architect also wanted a smaller one on the door. The mural showed every Creature on Scaffold Peaks, marching up the tower in a line. When she saw it, she laughed, because she had painted one Queuepillar upside down.
encounters.prompt: Which sentence should start Indi's paragraph?
encounters.success: It needs nothing before it. It introduces Indi and the mural, so 'it', 'she' and 'also' make sense later.

options.reason: 'It' and 'her' point back. The reader doesn't know who or what yet.

On the twelfth day, she finally climbed down and saw the whole thing for the first time.
options.reason: 'She' and 'the twelfth day' point back to earlier days. This can't come first.

options.text: The Architect also wanted a smaller one on the door.
options.reason: 'Also' and 'a smaller one' point back to something bigger. That must come first.

encounters.frame: A page from a whale-watching guide floated up to the Soggy Biscuit. The Queuepillars want it in order.
encounters.prompt: Put the guide's explanation in order.
encounters.success: Each sentence hooks onto the one before: this journey, those calves, freezing, this milk, fat enough, there.

items: Every winter, humpback whales leave the icy waters of Antarctica and swim thousands of kilometres north to warmer seas.
They make this enormous journey for one main reason: to give birth to their calves in calm, sheltered water.
Those calves are born with very little blubber, so they would freeze in the Antarctic water.
To stop them freezing, the mothers stay in the warm north until the calves have built up blubber on rich milk.
This milk is so thick and fatty that it looks a bit like toothpaste, and a calf drinks an enormous amount of it every day.
Once the calves are fat enough, the whales begin the long swim back south, towards Antarctica.
There, the hungry mothers finally feast on krill, after months without a proper meal.
body.reason: Start with the sentence that names the whales. Then follow: this journey, those calves, freezing, this milk, fat enough, there.

encounters.frame: The story of Scaffold Peaks' ladders is carved on a board, but the boards got stacked in the wrong order.
encounters.prompt: Put the history of the ladders in order.
encounters.success: Each sentence picks up the one before: instead of ladders, those ropes, the promise, keeping it, the spare.

items: When the Architect first arrived on Scaffold Peaks, there was not a single ladder on the whole island.
Instead, climbers had to haul themselves up the rock towers on ropes, which often snapped in the freezing wind.
After one of those snapped ropes left the Architect dangling over a cliff for an entire afternoon, a promise was made.
The promise was simple: every tower on the island would have a ladder by the following winter.
Keeping it meant building four hundred ladders in less than a year, mostly by hand.
By the first snowfall, there were four hundred and one, because the Architect had built a spare.
That spare ladder still leans against the ranger station, and nobody has ever worked out what it is for.
body.reason: Start where there are no ladders. Then follow: instead, those snapped ropes, the promise, keeping it, the spare.

encounters.frame: Gus is writing up his slime mould experiment. The Queuepillars are keeping their distance.
encounters.text: Gus's favourite living thing is not an animal or a plant. It is a slime mould, a bright yellow blob that creeps across rotting logs on the forest floor below Scaffold Peaks. It has no brain, no eyes and no legs, yet it can find food faster than most people can find their shoes. Gus scraped a lump of it off a log near the creek, carried it home in a lunchbox and gave it a name: Custard. He fed Custard on oat flakes, which it loves, and kept it in a dark cupboard, which it also loves. Mo was not allowed to open the cupboard, after he mistook Custard for dessert and got as far as reaching for a spoon. Gus says slime moulds have been around for hundreds of millions of years, and that some scientists use them to plan train lines, because they are so good at finding the quickest route between two places. For his science fair project, Gus wanted to prove that Custard was smarter than it looked. He drew a maze on a tray, put an oat flake at the end of every path and placed Custard at the entrance. Then he closed the cupboard door and waited.
encounters.prompt: Which sentence should come next in Gus's write-up?
encounters.success: 'Within two days' follows Gus closing the door and waiting. 'It' points back to Custard.

options.text: This second maze was even harder, with a dead end at every single turn.
options.reason: 'This second maze' needs a first maze to be finished. Gus has only just started the first.

options.text: As a result, Gus decided never to use oat flakes in an experiment again.
options.reason: 'As a result' needs something to have gone wrong. The test hasn't even happened yet.

options.text: Despite this, Mo still thought the yellow blob looked delicious.
options.reason: 'Despite this' needs a reason not to eat it just before. The last sentence is about waiting.

options.text: Within two days, it had found the shortest path to every oat flake.

encounters.frame: Tully wrote about the night the crew spotted a comet. One Queuepillar is marching the wrong way.
encounters.prompt: One sentence is in the wrong place. Tap it.

parts: Tully wrote this recount for the Peaks Star Club newsletter. She wrote it at midnight, wrapped in three blankets, and one sentence ended up in the wrong place. Every few thousand years, a comet called Frostwhisker swings past Earth, and this year it was due on the coldest night of winter. Tully had read that the best place in the whole archipelago to see it would be the summit of Scaffold Peaks, far from any town lights.

parts.reason: This is in the right place. Tully's plan comes straight after she reads about the summit.

parts.reason: This needs a telescope to carry. Look for the sentence where Tully gets one.

parts.reason: This is in the right place. Reaching the top follows the long climb.

parts.tap: Just after midnight, Frostwhisker appeared above the eastern ridge, trailing a tail like a silver scarf.
parts.reason: This is in the right place. The comet appears once they are at the top, under the clear sky.

Nobody spoke while it crossed the sky, not even Mo, who had brought a joke for the occasion.

parts: Mo wrote this recount for the camp newsletter. He was very proud of it, but when Tully read it out at breakfast the next day, everyone noticed that one sentence was in the wrong place.

parts.tap: On the first morning of camp, Mo was put in charge of breakfast for forty hungry Year 6 students.
parts.reason: This is in the right place. It needs nothing before it, so it starts the recount.

parts.tap: He decided to make his famous porridge, in a pot so large that he had to stand on a chair to stir it.
parts.reason: This is in the right place. 'He' and 'his famous porridge' follow Mo being put in charge of breakfast.

parts.tap: By the time he found the honey, the porridge had set as hard as cement.
parts.reason: 'Found the honey' needs Mo to go looking for honey first. Find that sentence and move it.

parts.tap: The camp leader had to chip it out of the pot with a hammer and a chisel.
parts.reason: This is in the right place. Chipping it out follows the porridge setting hard.

parts.tap: Those chips of porridge were so tough that Gus took three home to test as building bricks.
parts.reason: This is in the right place. 'Those chips' points back to the chipping.

parts.tap: Halfway through stirring, he climbed down to look for honey and left the pot bubbling on the stove.

parts: The students ate toast instead, and Mo was given a new job: washing up. He has since written a recipe for Cement Porridge. Nobody has asked for it.
